nodes.label: Fragments of Rum and the Ilkhanate
nodes.full: When the Ilkhanate disintegrated after 1335 and the last Seljuk sultan died in 1308, Anatolia split into a score of small states, each under a family of Turkmen chiefs who took a share of the old Seljuk and Mongol territory. It was an age of competing courts, small armies and a fluid frontier.
nodes.src: Cahen 1968; Ibn Battuta; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Karamanids
nodes.full: The Karamanids, a Turkmen dynasty of the Taurus, took Konya from the Mongol governors and ruled the central plateau and Cilicia for 175 years. Their rulers, Alaeddin Ali Bey, Mehmed Bey, Ibrahim and Pir Ahmed, were the main rivals of the Ottomans and kept the memory of the Seljuk state. Their capital was Karaman or Konya.
nodes.src: Şikari, Karamannâme; Aksarayi; Neşri; Cahen 1968; Yaşar Yücel on the Karamanids.

nodes.label: Turkish as language of state
nodes.full: A decree of the Karamanid Mehmed Bey in 1277 ordered that, from then on, no language but Turkish be used at court and in the offices. The beyliks wrote their deeds in Turkish more and more in the fourteenth century, and Turkish replaced Persian as the language of the chancery. It was the beginning of Turkish as a language of state in Anatolia.
nodes.src: Şikari, Karamannâme; Karamanid waqf deeds (Konya Museum); Cahen 1968.

nodes.label: Germiyan
nodes.full: The Germiyan emirs, the strongest of the western beyliks, ruled from Kütahya over the inner Aegean uplands, with the rich land and the mines. Their patronage of poets, including Ahmedi and Şeyhoğlu, made their court a centre of Turkish letters. Yakub II willed his lands to the Ottomans, who inherited them in 1428.
nodes.src: Neşri, Cihânnümâ; Ahmedi, Iskendername; Halil İnalcık on the Ottoman acquisition.

nodes.label: Ahmedi’s Iskendername
nodes.full: Ahmedi, a poet at the court of Germiyan and then of Bayezid I's son Süleyman Çelebi, wrote in Turkish verse the Iskendername, a universal history in some 8,000 couplets which told Alexander's story and the history of the Ottomans, the first Turkish epic in the Ottoman world.
nodes.src: Ahmedi, Iskendername (ed. Yavuz Pektaş); Kemal Silay, Ahmedi's Dasitan (1998).

nodes.label: Aydın and Umur Bey
nodes.full: Mehmed Bey of Aydın, with his sons, took the Maeander and Cayster valleys and the coast around Ephesus, Smyrna and Birgi from the Byzantines. His son Umur Bey (c. 1334–1348) was the great naval raider of the Aegean, an ally of John Kantakouzenos, who held Smyrna's harbour and fought the crusaders.
nodes.src: Enveri, Düstûrnâme; Ibn Battuta, Rihla; Elizabeth Zachariadou, Trade and Crusade (1983); Kantakouzenos, History.

nodes.label: Umur and Kantakouzenos
nodes.full: Umur Bey was a sworn friend of the Byzantine general John Kantakouzenos, to whom he sent troops in the civil war of 1341–1347. In Thrace his fleet and his men took part in the struggle for the throne, which brought Turkish soldiers into the Balkans. Umur and Kantakouzenos' friendship was said to be like that of brothers.
nodes.src: Kantakouzenos, History 2–3; Gregoras; Enveri; Zachariadou 1983.

nodes.label: Smyrna crusade
nodes.full: A naval league of Venice, the Hospitallers, Cyprus and the papacy took the harbour of Smyrna from Umur Bey in October 1344, a rare crusading success, and held its citadel for the next sixty years. Umur was killed in January 1348 when he tried to retake it. The fall of the greatest of the Aegean raiders ended the age of the emirates' sea power.
nodes.src: Enveri, Düstûrnâme; Kantakouzenos 4; Zachariadou 1983; Setton, The Papacy and the Levant vol. 1.

nodes.label: Fleets of the emirs
nodes.full: The emirs of the Aegean coast — Aydın, Menteşe, Saruhan and Karesi — built war fleets of galleys and smaller vessels from the forests of the coast and manned them with Turkmen and Greek crews. Umur Bey's fleet, of a hundred or more vessels, raided Thrace, the Cyclades and Crete as far as the Peloponnese. The skill of Byzantine and Italian shipwrights was adopted.
nodes.src: Enveri, Düstûrnâme; Kantakouzenos; Zachariadou 1983.

nodes.label: Captives of the raids
nodes.full: The emirs' raids on the Greek islands and coasts brought captives, who were sold at Smyrna and the coast to Venetian, Genoese and Cretan traders. Greek and Latin sources list thousands taken at a time, and Umur's slave market was a part of the emirates' economy. They are among the unrecorded victims of the age.
nodes.src: Kantakouzenos; Gregoras; Enveri; Zachariadou 1983.

nodes.label: Isa Bey Mosque
nodes.full: Isa Bey of Aydın built a great mosque at Ayasuluk beside the ruins of Ephesus in 1375, by a Syrian architect, Ali of Damascus, in a plan of two courtyards, with columns and marble from the ancient city. It is a major monument of the Aydınid state and of reuse of antique material.
nodes.src: Founder's inscription of the Isa Bey mosque (1375); Clive Foss, Ephesus after Antiquity (1979).

nodes.label: Menteşe
nodes.full: The Menteşe emirs held the Carian coast, Milas and Beçin and had a great fleet that raided the Dodecanese and Crete, and traded with Venetians. Their buildings at Milas and Miletus, the Ilyas Bey Mosque (1404) in particular, show a Turkish art meeting the antique stones of the region.
nodes.src: Zachariadou 1983; Paul Wittek, Das Fürstentum Mentesche (1934).

nodes.label: Saruhan and Karesi
nodes.full: The Saruhanids held Manisa (Magnesia) and the Hermus valley, and the Karesi emirs of Balıkesir the Troad and Mysia to the Marmara. Karesi's ghazi fleet and army were taken over by the Ottomans when Orhan absorbed it about 1345. Its officers, many of them, became Ottoman commanders and learned men.
nodes.src: Neşri; Aşıkpaşazade; İnalcık, The Ottoman Empire: The Classical Age (1973).

nodes.label: Treaties with Venice
nodes.full: Venice, anxious for its Aegean commerce, made agreements with Aydın, Menteşe and Saruhan in the 1330s and 1350s, which gave its merchants trading rights and a consul in exchange for payment, and arranged to pay a tribute for the safety of Crete and Negroponte. The emirates were a diplomatic power.
nodes.src: Venetian treaties with the emirs (Zachariadou, Trade and Crusade 1983); Documents of the Venetian archives.

nodes.label: Alum of Foça
nodes.full: The alum mines near Phocaea, held by the Genoese Zaccaria and then the Gattilusi, were the major source of alum, the mordant for dyeing cloth, for the wool industries of Italy and Flanders. Genoese and Venetian ships took it from the Aegean to the West. The trade tied the emirates to the western market.
nodes.src: Pegolotti, Pratica della mercatura; Philip Argenti, The Occupation of Chios by the Genoese (1958); Zachariadou 1983.

nodes.label: Eretnids, Kadi Burhan al-Din
nodes.full: When the Ilkhanate fell, Eretna, a Uighur officer, took Sivas and Kayseri and ruled Anatolia as the successor of the Ilkhans. After his dynasty weakened, Kadi Burhan al-Din, a judge, took the throne in 1381 and ruled in his own name, a ruler who wrote poetry in Turkish. He was killed in 1398 in battle with the Ak Koyunlu.
nodes.src: Aziz b. Ardashir Astarabadi, Bazm u razm; Kadi Burhan al-Din, Divan; Cahen 1968.

nodes.label: Candar
nodes.full: The Candar emirs (Isfendiyarids) held Kastamonu and the Paphlagonian forests, took Sinop in 1380 and the port of Samsun, and traded in timber, copper and ship stores. They survived the Ottoman wars with the help of their position until Mehmed II took Sinop in 1461.
nodes.src: Neşri; Chalkokondyles; Halil İnalcık, 'Candar'; Şehabeddin Tekindağ.

nodes.label: Dulkadir and Ramazan
nodes.full: The Dulkadirids at Elbistan and Maraş held the southeastern Taurus under Mamluk and then Ottoman suzerainty, and the Ramazanids of Adana and Tarsus kept Cilicia. Both were buffer states between the Mamluks and Ottomans in the fifteenth century and were bargained over in their wars.
nodes.src: Ibn Taghribirdi; al-Maqrizi; Yinanç, Dulkadir Beyliği (1989).

nodes.label: Akhis of Ankara
nodes.full: Ibn Battuta, who visited Ankara around 1332, found the city governed by an akhi, a head of the young men's brotherhood, and noticed that each town of Anatolia had akhi lodges which gave visitors food and shelter and defended the people. The akhis' control was strongest where state power was weakest.
nodes.src: Ibn Battuta, Rihla 2; Franz Taeschner, 'Akhi'; Suraiya Faroqhi on Ankara.

nodes.label: Ibn Battuta
nodes.full: The Moroccan traveller Ibn Battuta crossed Anatolia in the early 1330s from Antalya through Konya, Birgi, Magnesia and Sinope, and wrote of the akhis' hospitality, of the many principalities with their courts and of the tension between Turks and Greeks. His is the best view of the political map of the beyliks.
nodes.src: Ibn Battuta, Rihla (ed. Gibb, 1958–94).

nodes.label: Sisterhood of Rum
nodes.full: Ibn Battuta describes the women of Anatolia as unveiled and respected, and mentions a women's association, the Bacıyan-ı Rum, who gave hospitality to travellers in their lodges and served them with their own hands, in association with the akhis. They show a social role for women of the Turkmen towns.
nodes.src: Ibn Battuta, Rihla 2; Aflaki, Manaqib al-arifin; Suraiya Faroqhi, Towns and Townsmen of Ottoman Anatolia (1984).

nodes.label: Osman and Orhan
nodes.full: Osman, a frontier chieftain of Söğüt, defeated a Byzantine force at Bapheus in 1302 and took the countryside of Bithynia. His son Orhan took Bursa in 1326, Nicaea in 1331 and Nicomedia in 1337, absorbed Karesi in 1345 and crossed into Thrace. The state was a small frontier emirate among many.
nodes.src: Aşıkpaşazade, Tevârîh-i Âl-i Osmân; Neşri; Pachymeres; Kantakouzenos; Colin Imber, The Ottoman Empire 1300–1650 (2002).

nodes.label: Bapheus
nodes.full: Osman's Turkmen cavalry defeated a Byzantine force under the general George Mouzalon in the plain of Bapheus near Nicomedia, the first Ottoman victory recorded by Byzantine historians. The Greek peasants of Bithynia fled into the walled towns and the country was left to the Turks. It was the beginning of Ottoman expansion.
nodes.src: Pachymeres 10.25–26; Aşıkpaşazade; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Ghazi frontier
nodes.full: Osman's emirate grew on the frontier with the Byzantines in Bithynia, where warriors of the faith, ghazis, raided for booty and land. Paul Wittek (1938) saw the ghazi spirit as the Ottomans' motive force; later historians such as Cemal Kafadar and Rudi Lindner stressed their mixed, pragmatic and not exclusively religious nature.
nodes.src: Paul Wittek, The Rise of the Ottoman Empire (1938); Kafadar 1995; Lindner 1983.

nodes.label: Ottoman origin legend
nodes.full: The first Ottoman chronicles, written a century and a half after the events, give the story of Osman's dream of a tree growing from his body and shading the world, his descent from Oghuz Khan and his holy war on the Byzantines. They are a literature of legitimacy and a poor guide to the facts of the first century.
nodes.src: Aşıkpaşazade, Tevârîh-i Âl-i Osmân (c. 1484); Neşri, Cihânnümâ; Cemal Kafadar, Between Two Worlds (1995).

nodes.label: Nilüfer Hatun
nodes.full: Nilüfer, a Byzantine noblewoman, perhaps from Bilecik or Yarhisar, married Orhan and was the mother of Murad I. She founded a soup kitchen (imaret) in Iznik, which still bears her name. She represents the mixed background of the first Ottoman ruling family.
nodes.src: Aşıkpaşazade; Neşri; Kafadar 1995.

nodes.label: Çimpe
nodes.full: The Ottomans' first holdings in Europe were taken at Çimpe (Tzympe) in 1352, as a base given or taken in the civil war for Orhan's son Süleyman Pasha, who, after an earthquake destroyed the walls of Gallipoli in 1354, took that town too. The Ottomans had their bridgehead. They had been invited in as allies.
nodes.src: Kantakouzenos 4; Gregoras; Aşıkpaşazade; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Ottoman institutions
nodes.full: Orhan and Murad I put in place a kadi to every town, endowed mosques and zawiyas, and granted timars, small military fiefs, to cavalrymen. Murad, in the 1360s, began to take a fifth of the captives as the sultan's slaves and trained them as a new infantry, the janissaries, and a new body of administrators.
nodes.src: Aşıkpaşazade; Neşri; İnalcık 1973; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Mosques of Bursa
nodes.full: Bayezid I built the Ulu Cami of Bursa (1396–1399), a great hall with twenty domes on twelve piers, in a Seljuk manner. Mehmed I's Yeşil Cami (1419–1424) and the Green Tomb, with their turquoise tiles and carved portal, show the first Ottoman art with its own style. Bursa has been a UNESCO World Heritage site since 2014.
nodes.src: Ulu Cami and Yeşil Cami inscriptions; Godfrey Goodwin, A History of Ottoman Architecture (1971); UNESCO World Heritage List no. 1452.

nodes.label: Bursa and the silk road
nodes.full: Bursa, the first Ottoman capital, was the terminus of the caravans from Persia that brought raw silk, which the city's weavers made into cloth for Italy, Egypt and the Balkans. It had a silk market, Koza Han, built in 1491, and merchants from Genoa, Venice and Florence. The Ottomans' wealth began in this trade.
nodes.src: Halil İnalcık, 'Bursa and the commerce of the Levant' (1960); İnalcık and Quataert, An Economic and Social History of the Ottoman Empire (1994).

nodes.label: Murad I and Bayezid I
nodes.full: Murad I took Adrianople (Edirne) in the 1360s and made it the capital, defeated the Serbs at Maritsa in 1371 and the Balkan princes at Kosovo in 1389. Bayezid I, 'the Thunderbolt', took most of the Anatolian beyliks between 1390 and 1398, captured Karaman and Sivas and held Anatolia as far as the Euphrates, until his defeat by Timur.
nodes.src: Aşıkpaşazade; Neşri; Chalkokondyles; İnalcık 1973; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Absorption of the emirates
nodes.full: In 1390, in a swift campaign, Bayezid I took Aydın, Saruhan, Menteşe and Germiyan, then Hamid, and in 1397 or 1398 defeated the Karamanid Alaeddin Ali Bey at Akçay and took Konya. In 1398 he took Sivas and the country of the Eretnids. The emirs fled to Timur.
nodes.src: Aşıkpaşazade; Neşri; Chalkokondyles; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Ankara
nodes.full: Timur invaded Anatolia on the request of the dispossessed emirs and in a battle near Ankara destroyed Bayezid I's army, many of whose Anatolian troops had gone over to their old masters. Bayezid was captured and died in captivity. Timur restored the emirs to their territories and withdrew.
nodes.src: Sharaf al-Din Yazdi, Zafarnama; Chalkokondyles; Doukas; Clavijo, Embassy to Tamerlane; Marie Mathilde Alexandrescu-Dersca, La campagne de Timur en Anatolie (1942).

nodes.label: Interregnum
nodes.full: After Ankara the Ottoman lands were divided among Bayezid's sons, Süleyman, Isa, Musa and Mehmed, who fought each other until Mehmed Çelebi won in 1413. Anatolia's emirs, restored by Timur, recovered their lands. It could have been the end of the Ottomans, but their rivals were too weak and divided.
nodes.src: Doukas; Chalkokondyles; Dimitris Kastritsis, The Sons of Bayezid (2007).

nodes.label: Murad II and Mehmed II
nodes.full: After the sons of Bayezid fought each other until 1413, Mehmed I restored the state, Murad II took back the emirates one by one — Menteşe, Aydın, Germiyan, Hamid — and Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, Sinop and Trebizond in 1461 and, in the 1470s, much of Karaman. By 1481 the Ottoman empire held nearly all of Anatolia.
nodes.src: Neşri; Chalkokondyles; Kritovoulos; Doukas; İnalcık 1973.

nodes.label: Wars with Karaman
nodes.full: The Karamanids fought the Ottomans repeatedly from the 1380s, were beaten by Murad I at Frenkyazısı in 1386 and later sided with Timur and with the Crusaders. Mehmed II's campaigns of 1466 to 1474, under Gedik Ahmed Pasha, took Konya, and the last prince Pir Ahmed was driven out in 1483. The old Seljuk capital became Ottoman.
nodes.src: Şikari, Karamannâme; Neşri; Kritovoulos; İnalcık 1973.

nodes.label: Hatuniye Madrasa
nodes.full: Nefise Hatun, wife of the Karamanid Alaeddin Ali Bey, built a madrasa in Karaman in 1382 with a monumental portal of carved stone in the Seljuk tradition. The Karamanids' buildings in Karaman and Konya, such as the İmaret of Ibrahim Bey (1433), keep the style of thirteenth-century Konya.
nodes.src: Hatuniye waqf inscription (1382); Gönül Öney; Cahen 1968.

nodes.label: Otlukbeli
nodes.full: Mehmed II defeated Uzun Hasan, the lord of the Ak Koyunlu confederation, on the upper Euphrates in 1473, with the Ottoman artillery and janissaries against a larger Turkmen cavalry. The victory, which Uzun Hasan's Venetian allies had not expected, ended the danger of the Ak Koyunlu in Anatolia.
nodes.src: Kritovoulos; Neşri; Aşıkpaşazade; Woods, The Aqquyunlu (1976).

nodes.label: Ottoman–Mamluk war
nodes.full: When the Ottomans backed a rival Dulkadirid prince and took the Cilician plain's fortresses, the Mamluks fought them in a six-year war on the Taurus frontier, with sieges of Adana and Tarsus and a raid on Kayseri. It ended in a draw in 1491, the Ottomans being held for a generation.
nodes.src: Ibn Iyas; Ibn Taghribirdi; Shai Har-El, The Struggle for Domination in the Middle East (1995).

nodes.label: Bedreddin revolt
nodes.full: Bedreddin, a former kadi and Sufi who taught the sharing of property and the unity of faiths, was the author of a rising against Mehmed I in 1416, led by his disciples Börklüce Mustafa on the Karaburun peninsula and Torlak Kemal at Manisa. It was put down with cruelty and Bedreddin was hanged at Serres in 1420.
nodes.src: Şeyh Bedreddin, Varidat; Şerif'in Vakıa; Halil İnalcık; Michael Balivet, Islam mystique et révolution armée (1995).

nodes.label: Varidat
nodes.full: Bedreddin, a jurist and Sufi who was kadi askar at the court of Musa Çelebi, wrote the Varidat and other works on the unity of being, holding that God is all and that distinctions of faith and goods are illusions. His ideas inspired the revolt of 1416 and became a part of Anatolian dissent.
nodes.src: Şeyh Bedreddin, Varidat; Şeyh Bedreddin Simavna Kadısıoğlu; Michael Balivet 1995.

nodes.label: Hacı Bayram
nodes.full: Hacı Bayram, a village teacher from near Ankara and disciple of Hamid al-Din Aksarayi, became a spiritual master, with a large following among townspeople and craftsmen, and founded the Bayrami order. He was summoned to Edirne by Murad II and kept his independence. His tomb in Ankara stands beside the temple of Augustus.
nodes.src: Bayram Veli's biography (Hacı Bayram menakıbnamesi); Ahmet Yaşar Ocak; Faroqhi.

nodes.label: Mara Branković
nodes.full: Mara, daughter of the Serbian despot Đurađ Branković, married Murad II in 1435 as a seal of peace and remained a Christian. She was widowed in 1451, returned to Serbia, was a diplomat between her Serbian kin and Mehmed II and left her wealth to the monasteries of Mount Athos. She is a well-known figure of the Ottoman and Serbian courts.
nodes.src: Doukas; Chalkokondyles; Kritovoulos; Imber 2002.

nodes.label: Black Death
nodes.full: The plague of 1347 reached the Black Sea and Aegean ports from the Crimea and spread inland, with several waves later, devastating cities such as Bursa and Smyrna and the coast. It reduced the populations of the emirates and fostered the movement of Turkmen herds into depopulated land.
nodes.src: Michael Dols, The Black Death in the Middle East (1977); Ibn Battuta.

nodes.label: Turkmen flocks
nodes.full: Most of the beyliks' people were semi-nomadic Turkmen, who moved with sheep, goats and horses between summer and winter pastures, with their own tribal chiefs. The emirs drew soldiers from them and levied the sheep tax. Wool from the flocks was sold at Konya and Bursa.
nodes.src: Rudi Lindner, Nomads and Ottomans in Medieval Anatolia (1983); İnalcık 1973.

nodes.label: Ozan and kopuz
nodes.full: The Book of Dede Korkut, a collection of Oghuz tales set in the borderlands of Anatolia and the Caucasus and fixed in writing in the fifteenth century, tells of the ozan, the minstrel who sings the deeds of the heroes to the sound of the kopuz, a lute. The ozans, later called ashiks, were the poets of the Turkmen and of the Turkish folk tradition.
nodes.src: Kitab-i Dede Qorqut (Dresden and Vatican manuscripts); Geoffrey Lewis (trans., 1974).

nodes.label: Sabuncuoğlu
nodes.full: Şerafeddin Sabuncuoğlu, a surgeon at the hospital of Amasya, wrote in 1465 the Cerrahiyyetü'l-Haniyye, a work of surgery in Turkish, with some 190 miniatures showing operations and instruments, which draws on al-Zahrawi. It is the first illustrated surgical treatise in Turkish.
nodes.src: Sabuncuoğlu, Cerrahiyyetü'l-Haniyye (Paris, BnF, Turc 693); Uzel 1992.

nodes.label: The end of the Seljuks of Rum
nodes.full: The last Seljuk sultan, Masud II, died in 1308 and the Mongol governors did not appoint a successor, leaving the plateau to its Turkmen emirs.
nodes.src: background — see the Seljuks of Rum 1071–1308 folio (seljuks-of-rum-1071-1308)
